A canker is a destructive sore, wound, or area of decay that eats into living tissue — and crucially, it doesn't stay put. It tends to spread, grow worse, and damage more than just the spot where it started. Think of it as a kind of rot that creeps.

The word appears in several different contexts — human health, plants, animals, and even as a metaphor — but this central idea of a spreading, destructive wound or decay runs through all of them.
1. In the Human Body — The Canker Sore

The most everyday meaning you'll encounter is a canker sore: a small, painful ulcer that forms inside the mouth — on the inner lip, cheek, tongue, or the soft tissue of the gums.

Canker sores are:

  • Shallow and round, with a white or yellowish centre and a red border
  • Not on the outside of the lips (that's a cold sore, which is different — caused by a virus and contagious; canker sores are neither)
  • Painful out of proportion to their size — even a tiny one can sting sharply when eating, drinking, or speaking
  • Self-healing — they usually disappear on their own within one to two weeks

When someone says "I have a canker," they almost certainly mean one of these mouth sores.
2. In Plants and Trees — Plant Canker

In botany and gardening, a canker is a disease that causes areas of bark or woody tissue to die, crack, and sink. It typically looks like a sunken, discoloured patch on a branch or trunk — darker than the surrounding healthy bark, sometimes oozing, sometimes cracked open.

Key things to understand:

  • It is caused by fungi or bacteria that infect the plant, usually entering through a wound or weak spot
  • The dead area slowly expands outward, killing more tissue as it grows
  • If a canker grows large enough to go all the way around a branch (called girdling), it cuts off the flow of water and nutrients — and that branch dies
  • Common trees affected include apples, pears, roses, and many forest trees

Gardeners dread canker because it can disfigure or kill an otherwise healthy plant if not caught and cut away early.

The word also applies to certain animal diseases, though it refers to somewhat different conditions depending on the animal:

  • In horses: Canker is a disease of the hoof. It causes the tissue in the underside of the hoof (especially the frog — the rubbery V-shaped pad) to become soft, spongy, and foul-smelling, essentially rotting from the inside. It's difficult to treat and painful for the horse.
  • In dogs and cats: "Ear canker" is an older, informal term for a chronic ear infection or inflammation — the kind that causes a dog to shake its head and scratch at its ear persistently. Modern veterinarians tend to say ear infection or otitis, but canker is still used in everyday speech.
  • In birds (especially pigeons and birds of prey): Canker refers to an infection caused by a tiny parasite (Trichomonas gallinae) that creates yellowish, cheesy-looking lesions inside the mouth and throat. It can spread quickly through a flock and be fatal if it blocks the bird's airway.

In literature, formal writing, and thoughtful speech, canker is used figuratively to describe anything that corrupts, erodes, or spreads destructively within something that was once healthy — the way a real canker eats into living tissue.

Examples of how it's used:

  • "Corruption is the canker of this institution."
  • "Greed became a canker that slowly destroyed their friendship."
  • "Hatred is a canker that spreads if left untreated."

When used this way, the speaker is drawing on the word's original power: this isn't just a problem — it's something alive, spreading, and gradually consuming from within. It implies that if nothing is done, the damage will grow. The metaphor is old and powerful, and you'll find it often in Shakespeare, the King James Bible, and classic literature.

Across all these uses, a canker shares these qualities:

  • It is a wound, sore, or area of decay
  • It occurs in something living — a body, a plant, an animal, a society
  • It tends to spread or worsen if unaddressed
  • It destroys from within, not from an obvious external blow

That's canker: not just damage, but the kind that quietly eats away.
